An apothegm is a short, sharp, and clever saying that expresses a truth or a piece of wisdom — and it comes from a specific, identifiable person.

Think of it as a verbal dart: small, fast, and it hits the mark instantly.

For a saying to qualify as an apothegm, it needs to check all four of these boxes:

1. It is very short.
Usually just one sentence, sometimes even a single clause. No long explanations, no buildup. It is stripped down to the bone.

2. It is clever or witty.
It is phrased in a way that surprises you slightly, makes you think, or lands with a satisfying sting. The way it is said is almost as important as what it says.

3. It carries a truth or insight.
It is not just a funny quip. It says something meaningful about life, human nature, morality, or the world — something that feels true the moment you hear it.

4. It is attributed to a real, specific person.
This is the key thing that separates apothegms from proverbs and sayings. An apothegm has an author — usually a philosopher, a statesman, a writer, or some other notable figure.

"The unexamined life is not worth living." — Socrates

This is a classic apothegm. It is brief, thought-provoking, and it came from a specific person (Socrates). It tells you something profound about how humans should live — in just nine words.

"I can resist everything except temptation." — Oscar Wilde

Notice what makes this sharp: it sounds like it is about self-control, but then it playfully reverses your expectation at the last word. That twist is what makes it witty. And yet, underneath the humor, it actually says something true about human weakness. Short, clever, attributed — an apothegm.

"In the middle of every difficulty lies opportunity." — Albert Einstein

Brief, wise, coming from a specific person. An apothegm.
How Apothegm Compares to Similar Words

These words are close relatives, and mixing them up is very common. Here is how to tell them apart:

Proverb — A short, wise saying, but it is anonymous. Nobody knows exactly who said it. It comes from the collective wisdom of a culture, passed down across generations.

"Don't count your chickens before they hatch." — No one knows who said this first.

Apothegm — Also short and wise, but it has a known author. The fact that a specific person said it is part of what the word means.

Aphorism — Very similar to an apothegm. A short statement of a general truth. The difference is subtle: aphorisms tend to be more carefully written down and can be more formal or abstract, while apothegms are often more spontaneous remarks — things said aloud in a moment. Many sayings could honestly be called either one, and the words are sometimes used interchangeably in practice.

Maxim — A short statement of a rule or principle, especially about how one should behave. Maxims tend to be more prescriptive (telling you what to do) and a bit more formal in tone. They may or may not have a known author.

"Never put off till tomorrow what you can do today."

Epigram — A witty, pointed saying, often with a clever twist at the end. Epigrams lean heavily on the humor or irony, and many are written rather than spoken. Oscar Wilde was a master of epigrams.

The simplest shortcut: if it is short, wise, witty, and you know who said it — it is most likely an apothegm.

You will mostly encounter "apothegm" in literary, philosophical, or academic writing. People rarely use it in everyday casual conversation — they might just say "quote" or "saying" instead. But when a writer or scholar wants to be precise about the nature of a remark, they reach for "apothegm."

For example:

  • "The book is a collection of apothegms drawn from ancient Greek philosophers."
  • "He had a habit of speaking in apothegms — every sentence he uttered felt like something you should write down."
  • "Benjamin Franklin's writings are full of apothegms that people still repeat today."
The Single Best Way to Remember It

An apothegm = a short + smart + sharp saying from a known person.

If it has no known author, it is a proverb. If it has an author and it punches you in the brain in just a few words — it is an apothegm.
